title: Regional failover and capacity planning
summary: Foundry does not fail over for you. You pick a recovery tier, build the second region, size both for the load they must carry, set SLOs with an error budget, and rehearse the switch.
useIf: A regional incident would break your availability target, or a launch will multiply traffic.
avoidIf: Your availability target is low enough that a documented hot/cold recovery meets it.

explain.md: Foundry does not provide automatic failover or disaster recovery. Microsoft's guidance is two resources in two regions with two project connections, Service Health alerts and availability tests. It describes three tiers: **hot/hot** with an RTO of minutes and an RPO near zero, **hot/warm** with an RTO of 30 minutes to 2 hours, and **hot/cold** with an RTO of 2 to 8 hours [[r15]]. Global and Data Zone Standard are not a failover: if the primary region has an interruption, all traffic initially routed to it is affected, so they do not replace a second region [[r5]].

A second region must hold **quota and capacity**, and quota is not capacity [[r6]]. It starts with a **cold prompt cache**, because caches are per region. APIM counters are per gateway, not aggregated across regions [[r2]]. Residency may limit which region you can use. State kept in the primary resource does not follow you, so keep conversation state in a store you control (author synthesis).

Write **SLIs** first: time to first token p95, total latency p95 bucketed by output tokens, success rate excluding client quota errors, 429 and 503 rates, breaker open time, cache hit ratio and cost per successful task (author synthesis from the Azure latency guidance [[r27]]). An **error budget** is the rate at which the SLO may be missed; SLOs of 100% are neither realistic nor useful [[tr7]].

explain.title: Error budget
explain.expr: budget minutes = (1 - SLO) x minutes in the period
explain.example: 99.9% over 30 days leaves 43.2 minutes. A 40-minute regional outage burns 40 / 43.2 = 93% of it. A 99% SLO leaves 432 minutes (derived).

explain.title: A hot/warm two-region topology
explain.alt: A gateway routes to a primary region with a PTU deployment and standard spillover, and to a warm secondary region with its own deployment. Health probes feed the gateway.
explain.src:
flowchart LR
  U[Users] --> G[Gateway]
  G --> P[Primary region]
  G -.-> S[Secondary region]
  P --> PTU[PTU baseline]
  PTU --> SP[Standard spillover]
  S --> W[Warm deployment]
  H[Health probes] --> G

pitfalls.symptom: Failover works in a drill but the secondary returns 429 under load
pitfalls.cause: Quota or capacity in the secondary was sized for tests, not for the full peak
pitfalls.fix: Load test the secondary at full peak and hold quota and capacity for it

pitfalls.symptom: After failover, latency and cost jump
pitfalls.cause: The secondary starts with a cold prompt cache and a different deployment mix
pitfalls.fix: Budget for the jump, prewarm where supported, and watch cache hit ratio during failover

pitfalls.cause: State lived in the primary resource
pitfalls.fix: Keep session state in your own replicated store

pitfalls.cause: No health signal watches model errors, only the gateway
pitfalls.fix: Use availability tests, Service Health alerts and breaker state as inputs

scenarios.title: A 40-minute regional outage
scenarios.situation: A regional incident took an assistant offline for 40 minutes. The SLO is 99.9% monthly. The team has one region and Global Standard deployments.
constraints: Budget exists for modest standby cost
unknowns: Which second EU region has quota and capacity?
scenarios.question: What do you build?

options.name: Hot/warm in a second EU region behind the gateway, with a drill and a cold-cache budget
options.why: It brings the RTO to minutes to two hours at a standby cost the SLO justifies and keeps residency.
options.tradeoff: Idle capacity, a cold cache and a drill schedule.

options.name: Hot/cold runbook
options.why: Cheapest, with a 2 to 8 hour RTO.
options.tradeoff: One incident exceeds the monthly budget of 43.2 minutes by hours.

options.name: Add retries and a longer timeout
options.why: Retries cannot cross a dead region.
options.tradeoff: Retries are right for blips inside a healthy region.

scenarios.takeaway: Pick the tier from the SLO arithmetic, then prove it with a drill.

scenarios.title: An internal tool with a relaxed SLO
scenarios.situation: An internal research assistant serves 200 staff during working hours. The business accepts up to a few hours of downtime a month.
unknowns: Is there a documented owner for incidents?
Is quota in the backup region pre-approved?
scenarios.question: How much resilience do you buy?

options.name: Hot/cold: a runbook, pre-approved quota and an availability test
options.why: A 99% SLO allows 432 minutes a month, so a 2 to 8 hour recovery fits the arithmetic at low cost.
options.tradeoff: Slow recovery and a manual step.

options.name: Hot/hot across two regions
options.why: Double capacity for a tolerant SLO.
options.tradeoff: Right for a tight SLO and large traffic.

options.name: No plan; rely on the provider
options.tradeoff: Acceptable only if downtime has no business cost.

flips.then: Re-evaluate the SLO and move to hot/warm.
The runbook failed; invest in warm standby.

scenarios.takeaway: Match resilience spend to the error budget.

scenarios.title: A launch with five times the traffic
scenarios.situation: A launch in three weeks is expected to bring five times current traffic. Current peak is 400 RPM on PTU with Standard spillover.
constraints: Capacity in the region is unconfirmed
unknowns: What is the measured token mix and cache rate?
How fast can quota and capacity be added?
scenarios.question: What do you do first?

options.name: Re-run PTU sizing at 2,000 RPM, load test, create the larger deployment early to confirm capacity, and rehearse failover
options.why: Capacity is not guaranteed by quota or reservation, so creating the deployment early proves it exists.

options.name: Rely on spillover for the extra load
options.tradeoff: Standard quota may not cover 5x and latency varies.

options.name: Buy a one-year reservation and wait
options.tradeoff: Right after the deployment exists and utilization is known.

flips.if: A prefix redesign raises the cache rate
flips.then: Fewer PTUs are needed, so re-run the sizing.

flips.if: The launch is a one-day event
flips.then: Priority processing or spillover may beat a reservation.

scenarios.takeaway: Prove capacity before the launch, not during it.

quiz.q: Your SLO is 99.95% over a 30-day month. How many minutes of error budget do you have?
quiz.explain: (1 - 0.9995) x 43,200 = 21.6 minutes. A 40-minute outage uses 185% of that budget (derived) [[tr7]].

quiz.q: Match each tier to its documented recovery time.

pairs.r: RTO of minutes, RPO near zero

quiz.explain: These are the Foundry guidance tiers; they are approximate and you must verify them with drills [[r15]].

quiz.q: After failover latency and cost jump. Which is the most likely cause?
options: The secondary region starts with a cold prompt cache
quiz.explain: Prompt caches are per region, so the secondary starts cold and pays full prefill and input prices until it warms [[r25]]. Quota and retries are unrelated to the jump.

flashcards.back: No. Build two resources in two regions with two project connections, plus Service Health alerts and availability tests.
43.2 minutes. A 40-minute outage burns about 93% of it.

flashcards.front: What does failover cost that a drill may hide?
flashcards.back: A cold prompt cache, secondary quota and capacity that may be sized for tests, and state that lived in the primary region.
